The problem

Millions of warnings.
No detectable change.

In a 140-day randomised trial, over three million searches triggered a warning. Searching did not measurably fall. Yet people do want a way out, and cannot find one.

0
of 4,493 people surveyed said they wanted to stop

spread in help-click rates across four deployments: 0.0175% to 12.44%

A sign tells people to stop.
It doesn’t open a door.

Sources: Ahmia 140-day randomised field experiment, Ó Ciardha et al. 2026 (3.1M warnings, no detectable reduction in searching) · Insoll et al. 2024, JOTS 2(4) (n = 4,493; 266 sought help) · UNICRI research dossier, four-deployment table.
Our answer

A door, not a sign.

Doorway is a response layer a platform installs. When the platform’s own tools flag a search, the person meets a different card each time they come back, and every one leads somewhere.

Gate
What is this?
Fork
Where do I stand?
Wave
What do I do with this urge?
Hallway
What happens if I reach out?
CALL NOW
Door
Is it still open?
The platform decidesDoorway never detects anything and never sees what was typed. It hears only that a search was flagged.
Seven numbers, no personOnly aggregate counts leave the Door. No time of day, no identity, and small cells are hidden.
The moderator sees countsA Desk shows what was shown and how many reached for help, labelled as self-reported.
Why a different card each time is our design bet. It is not yet tested with visitors.
